issues.legal_issue: A concise pleading that identifiable occupants were unlawfully inducted into rented premises during the eviction suit sufficiently pleads unlawful subletting.
material_facts: The landlords amended their plaint to allege that the defendants, or any of them, had unlawfully inducted two identified defendants into the premises while the suit was pending.
The High Court held that this allegation was insufficient to plead unlawful subletting, although that objection had not been raised before the fact-finding courts.
issues.conclusion: The allegation was sufficient to give notice of the unlawful-induction claim, and the High Court erred in treating the pleading as inadequate.
issues.legal_principle: Order 6 Rule 2(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure requires a concise statement of material facts, not the evidence by which they will be proved. Order 6 Rule 5 permits the court to require further or better particulars and indicates that a suit should not be dismissed merely because particulars are lacking. Pleadings are intended to inform the other side of the case and identify the issues, not obstruct substantive justice. The Court relied on Manphul Singh v. Surinder Singh, AIR 1973 SC 2158, and M/s. Ganesh Trading Co. v. Moji Ram, AIR 1978 SC 484.

rule.if: rent_eviction_proceeding and pleading_identifies_occupants and pleading_alleges_induction and pleading_alleges_unlawfulness

predicates.rent_eviction_proceeding: The proceeding seeks eviction from rented premises.
predicates.pleading_identifies_occupants: The pleading identifies the occupants alleged to have been brought into the premises.
predicates.pleading_alleges_induction: The pleading states that the occupants were brought into possession of the premises.
predicates.pleading_alleges_unlawfulness: The pleading states that the occupants’ induction or possession was unlawful.

issues.definition: When an eviction pleading identifies the occupants and alleges both their induction into the premises and its unlawfulness, the pleading is sufficient for an unlawful-subletting claim.

issues.legal_issue: A High Court exercising supervisory jurisdiction should not set aside concurrent factual findings on the ground that a sufficiently pleaded eviction claim lacked detail, particularly when that objection was not raised before the fact-finding courts.
material_facts: The trial court found that an occupant had been inducted into the premises and that this amounted to unlawful subletting; the appellate authority confirmed the eviction decree.
The High Court set aside the concurrent findings based on its view that the plaint did not sufficiently plead subletting to that occupant.
The sufficiency of that pleading had not been considered or challenged before the two fact-finding forums.
issues.conclusion: The High Court exceeded its supervisory jurisdiction by upsetting the concurrent findings on that basis.
issues.legal_principle: Article 227 of the Constitution confers supervisory jurisdiction; it was not a proper basis to disturb concurrent factual findings on the fragile pleading ground relied on here, particularly when the point had not been raised before the fact-finding courts. The Court also applied the principles governing concise pleadings under Order 6 Rules 2 and 5 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

rule.if: supervisory_review_proceeding and concurrent_fact_findings and reversal_based_on_pleading_detail and pleading_objection_not_raised_below

predicates.supervisory_review_proceeding: The proceeding asks a higher court to exercise supervisory jurisdiction over a lower court’s decision.
predicates.concurrent_fact_findings: The trial court and the appellate fact-finding court reached the same factual findings.
predicates.reversal_based_on_pleading_detail: The supervisory court set aside those findings because it considered the pleading insufficiently detailed.
predicates.pleading_objection_not_raised_below: The sufficiency objection was not raised before the fact-finding courts.

issues.definition: When a supervisory court reverses concurrent factual findings for insufficient pleading detail on an objection not raised before the fact-finding courts, that interference exceeds its supervisory jurisdiction.

issues.legal_issue: A landlord who acknowledges the deceased original tenant but disputes which claimant inherited the tenancy cannot be nonsuited merely for declining to recognize a particular claimant as tenant while heirship is determined.
material_facts: The landlords pleaded that the deceased person had been their monthly tenant.
After the tenant and her mother died, a defendant claimed to be the tenant’s daughter and sole heir, while the landlords did not admit that claim and joined her as a party.
The trial court found that the claimant was the sole heir, and the landlords accepted that finding because they were not concerned with the dispute among competing claims to heirship.
issues.conclusion: The landlords’ cautious non-admission of the claimant’s heirship could not be used to nonsuit them; the High Court was wrong to find that they had not recognized the original tenancy.
issues.legal_principle: The Court treated the original tenant’s heirs as entitled to the tenancy right and held that a landlord who acknowledges the original tenancy may leave the identity of the legal heir to the court when heirship is uncertain. No earlier case or statutory provision was relied on for this point.

rule.if: rent_eviction_proceeding and original_tenant_acknowledged and heirship_uncertain and claimant_joined_for_heirship_determination

predicates.rent_eviction_proceeding: The proceeding seeks eviction from premises held under a tenancy.
predicates.original_tenant_acknowledged: The landlord states that the deceased person was the landlord’s tenant.
predicates.heirship_uncertain: The landlord does not know or accept which claimant inherited the tenancy after the tenant’s death.
predicates.claimant_joined_for_heirship_determinati: The claimant asserting inheritance is joined so the court can determine who inherited the tenancy.

issues.definition: When a landlord acknowledges the original tenancy, heirship is uncertain, and a claimant is joined for the court to determine heirship, the landlord cannot be nonsuited merely for not admitting that claimant as tenant.
